content.overview: A controller command or displayed status is not proof that equipment physically responded or the crop zone reached the intended condition. Specialists trace command, equipment state and measured response separately.

vocabulary.definition: Sequence from control request through equipment action to measured process response.
A condition that prevents or modifies operation until another required state is satisfied.
A signal that a monitored condition or system state meets defined criteria for attention or response.

sections.title: Command is not delivery
sections.body: A logged call for dehumidification does not prove the unit ran or moisture was removed. Verify equipment status and representative environmental response.

sections.title: Alarms need context
sections.body: Review alarm time, duration, device identity, process state and corroborating measurements. Repeated alarms can indicate capacity, sequencing, sensor or equipment-response problems.

sections.title: Never bypass safety to make controls look normal
sections.body: Do not defeat alarms, interlocks or safeguards to continue production or troubleshoot beyond authorization.

workedExamples: A dehumidifier command is active for 45 minutes, status never changes and RH remains high; the evidence supports equipment-response verification and escalation rather than assuming the command succeeded.
commonMistakes: Treating dashboard status as physical proof.
Resetting alarms repeatedly without preserving the event.
Bypassing an interlock to test equipment.
content.practicalApplication: Build a command-to-response timeline from a supplied controller/alarm trend and mark where evidence is missing.
content.summary: Control logic should be verified against physical response and crop-zone outcome.
